Series::sqrt¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::sqrt() const -> Series

What It Does¶

Applies the square-root transform elementwise.

For non-negative inputs, sqrt() returns the principal square root of each element. The shape is preserved and no broadcasting is involved.

Like Series::log, sqrt() is strongly domain-sensitive:

  • non-negative inputs produce ordinary real outputs

  • negative inputs produce nan

So this method teaches two ideas at once: a familiar numeric transform and the importance of validating the value domain before applying it blindly.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, where each element has been replaced by its square root.

Gradient¶

For positive inputs, sqrt() has a decreasing derivative:

  • the forward value is sqrt(x)

  • the backward multiplier is 1 / (2 * sqrt(x))

That means sensitivities are larger near zero and smaller for larger inputs.

Examples¶

Example 1. Perfect squares produce exact whole-number roots.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 4.0, 9.0}).sqrt());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 1.0000, 2.0000, 3.0000]

Example 2. The transform remains shape-preserving on matrices.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 4.0},
    {9.0, 16.0},
}).sqrt();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 2],
  [3, 4]]

Example 3. Reverse-mode sensitivity shrinks as the input grows.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 4.0, 9.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto out = x.sqrt();
out.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << out << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 3]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.5, 0.25, 0.16666667]

Example 4. Domain-edge behavior surfaces directly in the result.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({4.0, 0.0, -1.0}).sqrt();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 0, nan]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Negative inputs do not raise an exception in this verified path; they produce nan.

  • Zero is in-domain for the forward value, but it is still a numerically delicate point when you think about derivative behavior.

  • Because the derivative decreases with larger inputs, sqrt() can compress both values and sensitivities.

Summary¶

Teach sqrt() as a shape-preserving unary transform with a real-valued domain of non-negative inputs. It is a good method for showing how mathematically familiar functions still need explicit domain awareness in practical code.

See Also¶

  • Series::log: another domain-sensitive unary transform.

  • Series::exp: unary transform with the opposite growth profile.

  • Series::abs: often used upstream when you need non-negative magnitudes before further transforms.
